Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) are a class of drugs which act as competitive inhibitors at the MAO site. This prevents the break down of tyramine, which is normally broken down by MAO. With an increase in tyramine, a rise in catecholamines (such as noradrenaline and adrenaline) will occur, as tyramine is a precursor. This can lead to systemic sympathetic activation, such as tachycardia and high blood pressure. Alcohol will also interact with MAOIs, and this can cause a further rise in tyramine, leading to a greater rise in catecholamines. This can therefore cause the symptoms of over sympathetic activity.  Tryptophan is the precursor for serotonin, and tyrosine is the precursor for dopamine. These are not directly involved in the mechanism of the MAOIs. There is loss of transmission of pain and temperature signals from the body to the brain. However, the dorsal column pathways are located in the anterior portion of the spinal cord which was undamaged hence the intact 2-point discrimination, proprioception and vibratory senses.There is motor paralysis below the level of the lesion. In the anterior cord syndrome, the dorsal and ventral tracts are separated. The dorsal tract is responsible for carrying motor information and the ventral tract carries sensory information. The dorsal tract transmits to the next segment below the level of the lesion while the ventral tract transmits to the same segment below the level of the lesion resulting in motor paralysis below the level of the lesion. The reason the patient has an anterior cord syndrome is because it is the most common syndrome (especially in the elderly). It is caused by a hyperextension injury which results in widening of the canal space. This creates a compressive injury causing strokes in the anterior portion of the spinal cord. The strokes are usually transitional but can be vascular in origin. The literature states that in 60% of cases, the cause of the anterior cord syndrome is unknown.
